messages.content: I want to pack a healthier tiffin for myself, but I hate boring food.
Healthy does not have to mean boring. Colour and crunch make a big difference. What do you usually take now?
Mostly bread and jam, or chips if I'm in a hurry.

You could swap one thing at a time. Try a vegetable sandwich with a little chutney, or a roll made from last night's roti and sabzi. Add a fruit you like, such as a banana or a few grapes, for something sweet.
The roll idea is good. My mornings are rushed though.
Then fill the roll at night and keep it in the fridge. In the morning, you only need to pack it. A ready box takes less than a minute, which is faster than buying chips.
I broke my record in the 100 metre sprint today, but my coach says I still have a lot of work to do.
Congratulations on the record. That is a real achievement. Your coach is likely pushing you because he sees more potential in you.
It felt like he wasn't happy.
Coaches often focus on what to improve, because that's their job. You could ask him directly, 'What should I work on next?' That gives you something clear.
Good idea. I'll ask him on Monday.
That shows you want to grow, and coaches value that.
The teacher said I should speak louder, but I feel shy when everyone looks at me.
It's something many students work on. Try speaking to one friendly face in the room instead of the whole class.
I can try that.
Also, practise at home reading a paragraph aloud from a distance. Slowly raise your volume, until it's comfortable for someone across the room to hear you.
I want to move my study table next to the window, but my mom thinks it will be too bright.
Natural light is great for studying, and mid-day glare can bother the eyes. Which way does the window face?
East. So it's bright in the morning.
Then the table can work well, since morning light is gentle. A thin curtain can soften it if it ever gets too strong. Keep the screen or book at an angle, so the light doesn't glare on it.
I think our pet turtle looks lonely in his tank.
It's kind of you to care. Turtles are often fine on their own, but different kinds have different needs. Do you know which kind he is?
I'm not sure, the shop didn't say.
Then a local vet who looks after small animals can tell you, and advise about his tank. A vet is the best person to ask, since each kind has special needs.
Meanwhile, can I do anything for him?
Make sure he has clean water, a place to climb out and rest, and a proper light and warm spot. Ask the shop or the vet for those details.
He likes to stay under a rock. Is that bad?
Many turtles like a hiding place, so the rock is probably a good thing. If he stops eating or looks unwell, the vet is the person to call.
Okay. I'll ask the vet at the next visit. He's called Sheldon, by the way.
Sheldon is a great name for a turtle, calm and in no hurry. I hope the vet visit goes well.
I'm planning a surprise visit to my friend who is in a different town. Is that a good idea?
Surprises can be lovely, but people also need to be ready for visitors. Does she usually like surprises?
She does, but she may be busy.
Then maybe check with someone close to her about her schedule. You can still keep the exact time a surprise.
I can ask her sister.
Good thinking. Ask her sister to keep it quiet, and pick a time when your friend is likely to be at home.
What should I bring?
Something simple she likes, such as her favourite snack or a small plant. Your company is the main gift.
I forgot my homework at home and the teacher is strict. I'm scared.
That is a tough start to the day. The best step is to tell the teacher honestly before class begins, so you are not caught out later.
What do I say exactly?
Something simple: 'I am sorry, I forgot my homework at home. May I bring it tomorrow?' Say it calmly and look at the teacher while speaking.
What if they punish me anyway?
That may happen, and it would be hard. Honesty usually earns more respect than hiding the problem, though. Accept what the teacher says politely, and bring the work the next day.
How do I stop forgetting things?
Pack your bag the night before and check it against your timetable. Keep homework in the same pocket every day. Within a week, it becomes a habit.
I'm comparing two pairs of shoes, one cheaper and one sturdier. How do I choose?
Think about how often you will wear them and for what. For daily use or walking, a sturdy pair usually lasts longer, so it can cost less over time.
The cheaper pair looks nicer.
Looks matter, but fit and comfort matter more. Try both on and walk around the shop. Uncomfortable shoes tend to stay in the cupboard, however nice they look.
What if my feet are still growing?
Then a cheaper pair may be the sensible option, since you will outgrow either pair soon. Leave a little space at the toe, and check the fit again after a few months.
My father works long hours and we barely see each other.
That can feel lonely. It is natural to miss time with a parent. Does he know how you feel?
I haven't told him.
You could tell him when he has a quiet moment, saying that you miss spending time together. Most parents want to know.
What could we do together?
Small things count, such as having one meal a week together, a short walk or a game. It does not have to be big or expensive.
What if he's too tired?
Then something small and calm might suit him, like sitting together for a few minutes. Ask him what he would enjoy.
Thanks, I'll talk to him this weekend.
A weekend is a good time, since he may be more relaxed. Say it simply and kindly, and listen to what he says.
My bedroom door squeaks every time it opens.
A squeak usually comes from dry metal hinges rubbing together. Lubricating the hinge pin normally fixes it.
What can I use for that?
A drop of machine oil or a spray lubricant works well. In a pinch, rubbing a bar of soap or a candle on the pin helps. Wipe off any extra so it does not mark the door.
We have leftover chapatis. What can I make with them?
Cut them into strips and fry them with onions, tomatoes and spices for a quick chapati noodle dish. You can also tear them up and toss with curd or jaggery for a simple snack.
Can they be used for wraps?
Yes. Fill a chapati with vegetables or paneer and roll it up as a wrap. Warm it on a pan for a minute so the filling sticks together.
How long can the chapatis wait?
Cooked chapatis last about a day at room temperature in a covered box, or longer in the fridge. Use them soon and discard any that smell or look odd.
My science teacher, Mr Das, keeps saying I have talent but I never believe him.
It is kind of him to say that. Why do you think you find it hard to believe?
I only get average marks. I am Grace.
Marks do not show everything, Grace. A teacher sees how you ask questions, solve problems and think in class. Mr Das may notice things your marks do not show.
How can I find out what he sees in me?
Ask him directly after class. Say you would like to know where you are strong and where you can improve. Most teachers love a student who asks for feedback.
Good. What is my teacher's name again?
Your science teacher is Mr Das. You could ask him tomorrow, Grace, something like, "Sir, what do you think I do well, and what should I work on?"
Today is my birthday and nobody at home remembered. I am pretty down.
I am sorry, that must feel lonely. Happy birthday to you anyway. Have you told anyone that it is your birthday?
No, I did not want to ask for a wish.
I understand, but a gentle reminder is not begging. You could say, by the way, it is my birthday today, and see how they react. Family often forgets in a busy morning and feels bad later.
Okay, I might tell my mum at dinner.
That sounds like a good moment, when everyone is together. Say it lightly and let her respond. In the meantime, do something small for yourself, like a favourite snack or a walk.
I will get a jalebi on my way home. I do love jalebi.
A jalebi on your birthday is a lovely treat. Enjoy it slowly, and maybe share one with your mum at dinner when you tell her. It is a gentle way to open the conversation.
I sat next to a lovely old couple on the flight today. They told me about their travels.
That sounds like a nice surprise, and a good way to pass a flight. Where had they travelled in all those years?
They have visited forty countries. The lady, Mrs. Dsouza, said her favourite was Japan.
Forty countries is amazing. Did Mrs. Dsouza say why she loved Japan most? People who travel a lot often have good reasons.
She said the people were polite and the food was fresh, and the trains were always on time.
That is a lovely summary. If you ever go to Japan, you will have Mrs. Dsouza's story to remember. It might be worth writing down what she said in your travel notes.
I want to visit Japan someday because of what she said. What should I do first?

Start by learning a few Japanese phrases and reading about the things Mrs. Dsouza loved, like the polite people, the fresh food and the trains that always ran on time. Having a goal and a rough date makes a dream easier to reach.
Our class is planning a farewell trip, but the teachers are asking us to pick a place within a day's drive.
Good, a day trip is easier to manage. What kind of place does your class like? Is it nature, fun rides, or something to learn from?
Most want a water park. A few want a museum. I am in charge of collecting votes.
Then make a simple list on paper or a message, ask each classmate to choose one, and count the results. A fair method keeps everyone happy, even if their choice does not win.
The water park got nineteen votes. The museum got eight.
That is a clear result. Tell the class and the teachers the winner. Thank the museum supporters, and maybe suggest the museum for another outing so their idea is not forgotten.
Good idea. The teacher, Mrs. Fernandes, wants a list of names.
Then make a clean list in alphabetical order, and ask each student to confirm. Include parent contact numbers if the school needs them, so Mrs. Fernandes has everything in one place.
Done. Who did I say asked for the list, and which place won?
Mrs. Fernandes asked for the list of names, and the water park won the vote. Hand her the list soon so she can organise permission slips and the bus.
Karan here. I'd like to draw people in motion, like runners.
That is a challenging subject, Karan. Start with stick figures. Draw a line for the spine, a circle for the head and lines for arms and legs, bent to show the pose. Have you tried?
Not yet. My figures always look stiff.
Stiffness comes from straight lines. Draw the spine with a gentle curve, and bend the elbows and knees. Think of the body leaning in the direction of the run.
How can I see real movements?
Watch runners in a park, or ask a friend to hold running poses. Take quick sketches of one pose each, spending only thirty seconds on each. Fast sketches catch the motion.
Maybe my friend Dev can pose for me. He runs every day.
That would be perfect. Ask Dev to pause in a running stance for a few seconds, and draw the curve of his spine and bent knees first.
Who did I say would pose?
You said your friend Dev, Karan. Since he runs every day, he will know good running poses. Start each sketch with a curved spine and bent knees.
I started a weekend job at a bookshop. The owner, Mr. Rao, wants me to arrange the new stock.
That sounds like a pleasant weekend job. Arranging new stock is a good way to learn where everything lives. Take your time and keep similar books together so customers can find them.
Mr. Rao said to put the school textbooks near the door, because students come in first for those.
That is sensible. Putting the textbooks near the door means students find them quickly and do not need to ask. Keep the heavy ones on lower shelves so they are easy to lift.
What if a student asks for a textbook I can't find near the door?
Be honest and polite. Say you will check, then ask Mr. Rao or look at the stock list. Since he wanted the textbooks near the door, tell him about any missing title so he can restock it.
Varun at my office keeps eating lunch alone and I think he's lonely. I've never really spoken to him.
It is kind that you noticed. You do not need a big gesture. Start with a simple, friendly hello, or ask if he would like to join you for lunch.
What if he says no?
Then smile and say maybe another day. Some people need a few invitations before they feel comfortable. Saying no today does not mean he did not appreciate it.
I'll ask Varun to join me tomorrow. What can I talk about, since he always eats alone?

Ask something light, like what he usually eats or how his week is going. Since Varun is used to eating alone, keep it easy and short, so he does not feel pressured, and let him answer at his own pace.
I want to invite my neighbours for chai on Sunday. Is that a good idea?
It is a lovely idea. A small chai evening is an easy way to know your neighbours better. How many families live nearby, and do you have space at home for them?
Three families on our floor. I have a small living room.
Then keep it simple. Invite them for an hour in the late afternoon, serve chai and a few biscuits, and perhaps move a couple of chairs from the bedroom so everyone can sit.
One family is Gauri's, she has a baby. Is that a problem?
Not at all, but think about the baby. Keep the room quiet, put small things out of reach, and give Gauri a comfortable seat where she can keep the baby close.
Good point. Should I send a message or knock on their doors?
Knocking on the door is warmer, and it lets you say hello in person. If someone is out, leave a short note with the day and time of the invitation.
I will knock this evening. What should I remember about Gauri?
Remember that Gauri has a baby, so offer her a comfortable seat and keep the room calm and tidy. Keep hot cups of chai well out of the baby's reach.
I'm moving to a new school next month. Ishita says it will be fun but I'm not sure.
Moving is a big change, so mixed feelings are completely normal. Ishita sounds supportive. What worries you the most?
Making friends. I am not good at starting conversations.
Many students feel the same. You do not need a big speech. A simple hello, a compliment on a pencil box, or asking where the library is can be enough to start.
I'll try the library question. Maybe I'll ask Ishita to practise with me.
That is a great way to practise. Ask Ishita to pretend to be a new classmate, and say your question out loud a few times until it feels easy.
